title: GOD’S ANSWER TO SEXUAL TEMPTATION ISN’T PRETENDING DESIRE DOESN’T EXIST
paragraphs:
GOD’S ANSWER TO SEXUAL TEMPTATION ISN’T PRETENDING DESIRE DOESN’T EXIST
The desire you are ashamed to admit may be the very battlefield where Jesus teaches you that holiness is not becoming less human—it is learning whom your humanity belongs to.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that happens when you love Jesus...
and still feel temptation.
You prayed.
You worshiped.
You meant every word when you told God, “I want to be pure.”
Then something appeared on your screen.
Someone walked past you.
A memory resurfaced.
Your marriage became difficult.
Loneliness settled into the room.
Your body responded before your theology had time to speak.
And suddenly you were ashamed—not only because you were tempted, but because somewhere along the way you began believing that genuinely holy people simply stopped experiencing desire.
So you wondered...
What is wrong with me?
Maybe nothing is wrong with the fact that you noticed.
Maybe the real question is what you will do next.

Because Scripture never teaches that sanctification turns human beings into people incapable of experiencing temptation. Jesus Himself “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15, KJV).
Read those final words again.
Yet without sin.
Temptation and sin cannot therefore be identical.
That distinction could rescue someone from years of unnecessary shame.
Jesus does not command you to pretend your body has no impulses. He calls you to refuse to make those impulses your master.
And that difference matters.

Sexual desire itself is not some contaminant that entered creation when humanity fell. Before Genesis ever records the serpent, shame, hiding, adultery, pornography, exploitation, or lust, God created humanity male and female and established the one-flesh union of marriage.
Then Scripture says something our shame sometimes struggles to believe:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” — Genesis 2:25, KJV
Naked.
Unashamed.
Before sin distorted sexuality, sexuality was not dirty.
God created the body.
God created marriage.
God created intimacy.
God created human beings capable of desire.
Sin did not invent desire.
Sin disorders desire.

That is why Christianity is not fundamentally a campaign to destroy human longing. The Gospel reaches deeper. Christ begins restoring people whose loves, appetites, imaginations, bodies, relationships, and desires have been disordered by sin.
And this is where some believers have quietly suffered.
We sometimes tell people what not to do without teaching them what holiness actually is.
Don’t look.
Don’t touch.
Don’t fantasize.
Don’t sleep with them.
Don’t watch that.
All of those boundaries can matter enormously.
But Scripture gives us something richer than a Christianity built entirely around the word don’t.
Listen carefully to Paul:
“Τὰς δὲ νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας φεῦγε· δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην, πίστιν, ἀγάπην, εἰρήνην...”
“Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace...” — 2 Timothy 2:22, KJV
There are two movements in that sentence.
φεῦγε — pheuge.
Flee.
Run.
Get away.
Do not negotiate with what is pulling you toward sin.
But then comes another command:
δίωκε — diōke.
Pursue.
Chase after.
Paul does not merely say, “Run away from sinful desire.”
He essentially says:
Run from this... toward that.
Toward righteousness.
Toward faith.
Toward love.
Toward peace.
Toward believers who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.
Biblical purity is therefore not merely the absence of sexual sin.
It is the presence of a greater pursuit.
You were never meant to spend your entire Christian life staring backward at the temptation you are trying not to commit.
You were meant to run toward Christ.
And perhaps that changes the battle.
Because some people reading this have been fighting sexual temptation through sheer terror.
You wake up thinking about what you must not do.
You spend the afternoon trying not to think about it.
You lie down wondering whether tonight will be another failure.
You fall.
You repent.
You promise.
You fail.
You cry.
You delete everything.
You reinstall everything.
You pray harder.
You hide deeper.
Sunday arrives, and you sing beside people who have absolutely no idea what happened Saturday night.
Then shame whispers:
If these people knew you, they would never look at you the same way.
And perhaps the cruelest whisper comes afterward:
God must be tired of you too.
But listen to the Gospel.
The answer to your sin is not pretending sin is harmless.
And the answer is not pretending temptation does not exist.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
The One who knew exactly what He was purchasing when He went to the cross.
Not the polished version of you.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version with the browser history cleaned up.
You.
The sinner.
The struggler.
The person who has made promises and broken them.
The person who may genuinely love God while simultaneously discovering how deeply sin has trained the heart to seek comfort in places that cannot save.
Christ did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was so devastating that nothing less than the blood of the Son of God could reconcile sinners to God.
That means grace is not God saying sexual sin does not matter.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do for themselves.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
This is where scandal becomes grace.
You brought guilt.
Christ brings righteousness.
You brought rebellion.
Christ brings reconciliation.
You brought what you were ashamed to expose.
Christ brings wounds in His hands.
And because Jesus rewrites everything, repentance does not mean you pretend yesterday never happened.
It means yesterday no longer gets to be your lord.
Maybe you need to hear something painfully practical.
When temptation comes, stop being shocked that you are being tempted.
Recognize the battlefield.
Paul wrote:
“πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος...”
“No temptation has overtaken you except what is common to humanity.”
The Greek word πειρασμός — peirasmos can refer to temptation or testing depending upon context.
Paul's point in 1 Corinthians 10:13 is not that temptation is imaginary.
Quite the opposite.
It is real.
Human.
Recognizable.
And then comes the center of the promise:
πιστὸς... ὁ Θεός — pistos... ho Theos.
God is faithful.
Notice where Paul puts your hope.
Not:
You are strong enough.
Not:
You have enough willpower.
Not:
Real Christians never struggle.
God is faithful.
And Scripture says that with the temptation He provides ἔκβασιν — ekbasin, a way out, so that it may be endured.
Sometimes that “way out” looks remarkably ordinary.
Put the phone down.
Leave the room.
End the conversation.
Stop feeding the fantasy.
Install accountability.
Tell a mature believer the truth.
Do not meet that person alone.
Go to sleep instead of scrolling at 1:30 in the morning.
Stop revisiting the profile.
Stop convincing yourself that because you have not physically committed adultery, repeatedly cultivating desire for someone who is not your spouse is spiritually harmless.
Jesus takes the inner life seriously.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He moves beyond the external prohibition of adultery and confronts the deliberate lustful gaze of the heart.
Christ is not teaching that merely recognizing another person's attractiveness is adultery.
He is confronting the heart that intentionally turns another human being into an object for covetous sexual desire.
That distinction matters because otherwise sensitive Christians can become terrified by every involuntary thought or physical response.
You cannot always control the first thing that enters your awareness.
You can decide whether you invite it to dinner.
There is a difference between noticing and nurturing.
Between temptation arriving and temptation being entertained.
Between desire appearing and desire being enthroned.
You may not control every knock at the door.
But by the grace of God, you do not have to hand every visitor the keys to the house.
This is why Paul becomes startlingly direct about sexual immorality:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The command is not:
Study how close you can stand to it.
Determine precisely how much you can watch without technically crossing the line.
See how emotionally intimate you can become with someone else's spouse.
Keep the secret conversation because “nothing has happened.”
Keep the app because you are “stronger now.”
Paul says:
Flee.
Joseph did not remain in Potiphar's house giving himself a motivational speech.
He ran.
Sometimes holiness looks profoundly undignified.
Sometimes victory is leaving.
Sometimes spiritual maturity is admitting, “I cannot keep putting myself here and pretending I am invincible.”
Sometimes the most courageous thing a Christian can do is run.
But remember Paul's other word.
Pursue.
Because if you only remove the pornography without confronting the loneliness underneath it, another counterfeit comfort may eventually replace it.
If you only stop the affair without rebuilding honesty, affection, accountability, and covenant faithfulness, the heart may remain hungry for the same poison in another bottle.

If you only suppress desire while never learning to see another person as someone bearing God's image rather than existing for your consumption, you have changed behavior without necessarily retraining love.
Christian purity is not learning to hate the body.
It is learning to honor God with it.
Paul says your body is not meaningless.
“For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body...” — 1 Corinthians 6:20, KJV
Bought.
With.
A.
Price.
Your body belongs to Jesus.
Your eyes belong to Jesus.
Your imagination belongs to Jesus.
Your sexuality belongs to Jesus.
Your singleness belongs to Jesus.
Your marriage belongs to Jesus.
Your loneliness belongs to Jesus.
Even the part of your life you are most embarrassed to discuss belongs beneath the lordship of Jesus.
And perhaps tonight you do not need another promise that begins, “God, I swear I will never struggle again.”
Perhaps you need a more truthful prayer.
“Jesus, this desire is here.
You already know it.
I will not hide it from You.
I will not call sin holy, but neither will I pretend temptation means You have abandoned me.
Show me the escape.
Give me strength to take it.
Teach me what I am actually seeking beneath this temptation.
Comfort?
Validation?
Intimacy?
Control?
Escape?
To feel wanted?
And teach my heart to seek in You what sin keeps promising but can never finally give.”
Because sexual temptation frequently promises more than sex.
It whispers:
You will finally feel wanted.
You won't feel lonely tonight.
Someone desires you.
You deserve this.
Just escape for a few minutes.
Then afterward comes the invoice.
Secrecy.
Distance.
Shame.
Escalation.
Broken trust.
A divided heart.
Sometimes shattered families.
Sin advertises the moment.
It hides the aftermath.
Jesus does something completely different.
He tells you the cost of discipleship openly—and then gives you Himself.
He does not merely say, “Stop wanting.”
He says, in effect:
There is something greater to want.
“Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.” — Matthew 5:8, KJV
They shall see God.
That is the destination.
Not merely a clean browser history.
Not merely another thirty-day streak.
Not merely avoiding scandal.
God.
Knowing Him.
Loving Him.
Becoming increasingly free to see people as people instead of products for your appetite.
Learning faithfulness when nobody applauds.
Becoming the same person behind a locked door that you appear to be beneath church lights.
And when you fall?
Do not redefine sin.
Do not excuse it.
Do not make peace with it.
But do not run from Christ because you sinned against Christ.
Run to Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Confession is the death of pretending.
Repentance says:
I did this.
Grace says:
Come into the light.
Repentance says:
This must change.
Grace says:
You will not change yourself apart from Christ.
Repentance is not self-hatred.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And Christian community belongs in this story too.
Remember Paul's words:
“...with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.”
You were not designed to fight every battle alone.
Secrecy gives temptation oxygen.
Honest Christian fellowship can drag hidden things into daylight.
Find mature, trustworthy believers who care more about your holiness than your image.

If you are married and sexual sin has damaged your covenant, honesty and restoration may require wisdom, patience, pastoral care, and sometimes qualified counseling. Consequences do not magically disappear because forgiveness is real.
Grace is not pretending wounds never happened.
Grace is Christ meeting sinners in the wreckage and teaching them to walk in truth.
And maybe this article found you while you are standing inside that wreckage.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does know.
Maybe the relationship ended but your conscience still screams.
Maybe pornography has followed you since adolescence.
Maybe you are single and exhausted by being told simply to “wait,” as though loneliness does not ache.
Maybe you have remained sexually faithful outwardly while privately feeding fantasies you would be horrified for anyone to see.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you never would.
Then hear this carefully.
Your sexual history is not more powerful than the blood of Jesus Christ.
That sentence does not make sin small.
It makes Christ enormous.
Paul wrote to Corinth—a church surrounded by sexual disorder—and after naming serious sins, he said:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus...” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
Such were some of you.
There are few words more beautiful for a repentant sinner.
Were.
Not because they had never sinned.
Because Jesus changes the relationship between the redeemed sinner and the old identity.
The Gospel does not say:
Pretend the scandal never existed.
The Gospel says:
The scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So if you are fighting tonight, fight.
If you need to flee, flee.
If you need to confess, confess.
If you need accountability, seek it.
If you have sinned, repent.
If someone needs forgiveness from you, pursue what truthful restoration requires.
If you have fallen a hundred times, do not use grace as permission for number 101.
Use your need for grace as another reason to throw yourself upon Christ.
And if you are still standing, do not become proud.
The reason you stand is grace too.
Maybe someone reading this needs permission to finally stop hiding.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing even a small confession into the light becomes the first crack in a wall you have spent years building.
Then pray for someone else in those comments.
Remind somebody that repentance is possible.
Remind somebody that forgiveness is real.
Remind somebody that holiness is worth pursuing.
Because there is probably someone scrolling through Facebook tonight who thinks he is the only Christian fighting this.
There is probably a woman quietly convinced her hidden struggle makes her uniquely disgusting.
There is probably a husband drifting toward a decision that could wound his family.
There is probably a teenager learning sexuality from an algorithm before anyone has lovingly shown them God's design.
There is probably a believer one click away from returning to something Christ has been teaching them to leave behind.
Not as a badge announcing that you have conquered temptation.
Share it as a hand reaching backward toward somebody still trapped in the dark.
We do not buy grace. We receive salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Someone you know may be hiding a battle they have never had the courage to name.
Your share may become the doorway through which they discover they are not alone—and, far more importantly, that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Sexual temptation does not prove Christ has abandoned you.
It reminds you that you still need Him.
So stop pretending desire does not exist.
Bring it beneath His lordship.
Flee what corrupts it.
Pursue what makes you more like Christ.
Confess what you have hidden.
Receive the grace you cannot manufacture.
Walk with people who call upon Jesus from a pure heart.
And keep your eyes on the Savior who did not come merely to make scandalous people look respectable.
He came to make dead people alive.
The thing you thought would become the darkest final sentence of your story may become the very place where the scars of Christ teach you that grace still knows how to write.
